title: Shopify vs Custom Build: How to Choose Your E-commerce Stack in 2026
metaTitle: Shopify vs Custom Build: E-commerce Stack 2026 | TDM
metaDescription: An honest comparison of Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento and custom Next.js/Laravel builds: real costs, limits, migration paths and how to choose in 2026.
excerpt: Most stack debates are argued by people selling one of the options. Here is an honest comparison of Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento and custom builds: including what each actually costs to own, and when switching makes sense.

faqs.q: Is Shopify still the best e-commerce platform in 2026?
faqs.a: For most standard retail brands, yes: Shopify remains the correct default because it removes hosting, security, checkout and compliance work at a reliability level custom builds rarely match on similar budgets. It stops being the right answer when your business model fights its constraints: complex B2B pricing, marketplaces, heavy customization, or app fees that outgrow engineering costs.

faqs.q: When is a custom e-commerce build worth the cost?
faqs.a: A custom build (typically Next.js or Laravel) is worth it when commerce is part of a larger product like a marketplace or SaaS, when performance at high traffic provably drives revenue, when platform fees at volume exceed engineering costs, or when a differentiated buying experience is your competitive moat. It requires a permanent engineering budget: custom commerce without ongoing development decays from day one.

faqs.q: What does an e-commerce site really cost over three years?
faqs.a: As rough three-year totals: a Shopify SMB store runs $15,000-$60,000 including apps and theme work; WooCommerce is cheaper at rest but adds hosting and maintenance retainers; Magento typically reaches six figures once development and hosting are counted; custom builds start at $40,000-$150,000 to launch plus $2,000-$10,000+ monthly in ongoing engineering.

faqs.q: Will migrating platforms hurt my SEO?
faqs.a: Only if it is done carelessly. The critical work is mapping every existing URL to a 301 redirect, re-implementing structured data, and monitoring rankings through cutover. Plan the redirect map before development starts: a sloppy replatform can erase years of organic equity in a week, while a disciplined one typically holds or improves rankings within a few months.

body:
Ask a Shopify agency what platform you need and the answer is Shopify. Ask a dev shop and the answer is custom. Both answers are sometimes right, which is exactly why neither is useful on its own. We build on Shopify, WordPress, Magento and custom stacks, which puts us in the rare position of having no platform to defend, so this is the comparison we give clients before any code gets written.

The honest starting point: for most merchants, most of the time, Shopify is the correct default in 2026. The interesting questions are where its edges are, and what to do when you hit them.

## Shopify: Strengths and Real Limits

### Where Shopify earns its dominance

Shopify's core value is that it removes entire categories of work. Hosting, security patching, PCI compliance, checkout infrastructure, CDN, fraud tooling: all handled, at a reliability level almost no custom team matches on a comparable budget. Its checkout is among the highest-converting in the industry, and Shop Pay demonstrably lifts conversion versus guest checkout. The app ecosystem covers nearly any feature a standard retail business needs, and the admin is simple enough that marketing teams run daily operations without developers. Time-to-launch for a well-scoped store is weeks, not months.

### Where the limits show up

The costs of Shopify are structural, and they arrive on a schedule. App stacking is the first: features arrive via third-party apps at $20-$300 each per month, and mature stores commonly carry $500-$2,000 monthly in app fees, with each app adding scripts that drag site speed. Checkout customization is tightly constrained outside Shopify Plus, and even Plus has boundaries. Complex product logic (configurable manufacturing, B2B price lists per customer, multi-vendor marketplaces, unusual subscription mechanics) fights the platform's data model. Transaction fees apply when you avoid Shopify Payments, which matters in markets where local gateways are mandatory. URL structure and some technical SEO controls are fixed, and internationalization beyond Shopify Markets' assumptions gets awkward. None of these are dealbreakers for a standard retail brand; each can become one for a business whose model does not fit the mold.

## Where WooCommerce and Magento Fit

### WordPress / WooCommerce

WooCommerce remains the right call for content-led commerce: stores whose growth engine is SEO and editorial, where the blog is not an appendix but the acquisition strategy. You get WordPress's unmatched content tooling, full ownership of code and data, no platform fees, and cheap extensibility through the largest plugin ecosystem in existence. The trade is operational: you now own hosting, performance, security and updates, and a neglected WooCommerce store degrades in a way a neglected Shopify store does not. It suits merchants with development support (in-house or through a partner) and content ambitions that Shopify's blogging tools genuinely cannot serve.

### Magento (Adobe Commerce)

Magento is a heavyweight: overkill for most, irreplaceable for some. Its native strengths (multi-store from one backend, granular B2B features, complex catalog and pricing rules, deep ERP integration) matter to established mid-market and enterprise merchants with catalogs and org structures Shopify strains to model. The price is real: Magento demands experienced developers, serious hosting and ongoing maintenance budgets. Choose it when the business complexity genuinely requires it, and only with committed technical resourcing. Choosing Magento to 'grow into' is one of the most expensive mistakes in e-commerce.

## When Custom (Next.js / Laravel) Is Worth It

A custom build: typically a Next.js storefront over a headless commerce backend, or a Laravel application owning the full stack: is the most powerful and most expensive option. It is worth it in a few specific situations.

First, when commerce is only part of the product: booking plus retail, marketplaces with vendor onboarding, commerce embedded in a SaaS or service platform. Platforms model stores; they do not model your business logic. Second, at scale where performance is provably revenue: a sub-second, fully controlled storefront with edge rendering can be worth seven figures annually to a high-traffic brand, and you cannot buy that level of control from a theme. Third, when platform fees at volume exceed engineering costs: the arithmetic flips for some Plus-tier merchants. Fourth, when differentiated experience is the moat: configurators, personalization, custom checkout flows that platforms will never permit.

The honest counterweight: a custom build means you own everything, forever. Every feature Shopify ships free, your team builds and maintains. Budget not just the build but a permanent engineering line item. Custom commerce with no ongoing development budget is a depreciating asset from day one.

## Migration Paths

Stacks are not marriages. The common migrations we see, in order of frequency: WooCommerce to Shopify, usually to shed maintenance burden as a brand scales past its operational appetite; Magento to Shopify Plus, trading flexibility for lower total cost when the complexity Magento served has been simplified out of the business; and Shopify to headless or custom, keeping Shopify as the commerce engine while replacing the storefront with Next.js for speed, content and control: a path that de-risks the jump because checkout and operations stay put.

Whatever the direction, the migration risks are constant: SEO and order history. Every URL must be mapped and 301-redirected, structured data re-implemented, and rankings monitored through the cutover; done carelessly, a replatform can erase years of organic equity in a week. Plan the redirect map before the build starts, not after.

## Total Cost of Ownership: The Comparison That Matters

Sticker prices mislead; compare three-year ownership. A Shopify store runs subscription plus apps plus theme work (commonly $15,000-$60,000 over three years for an SMB, more on Plus) with near-zero infrastructure risk. WooCommerce trades subscription fees for hosting and maintenance retainers; cheaper at rest, more variable, and dependent on disciplined upkeep. Magento starts around six figures over three years once licenses (for Adobe Commerce), development and hosting are counted. Custom builds start at $40,000-$150,000+ to launch and carry ongoing engineering of $2,000-$10,000+ monthly, in exchange for zero platform constraints and full asset ownership.

The decision rule we give clients: choose Shopify unless you can name the specific, current (not hypothetical) requirement it cannot meet. Choose WooCommerce when content is the growth engine and you have real technical support. Choose Magento only when its complexity maps to complexity your business already has. Go custom when commerce is your product, not just your channel, and you are prepared to fund engineering indefinitely.

If you are weighing a build or a migration, our /development/ team scopes these decisions platform-neutrally: because we ship on all four stacks, the recommendation is based on your requirements and your three-year math, not on what we happen to sell.
